abstract: Animal genomes are organized into chromatin loops and topologically associating domains. Cohesin drives loop extrusion, and the architectural factor CTCF halts loop-extruding cohesin. CTCF-anchored loops facilitate interactions between distal cis-regulatory elements and regulate gene expression. However, when CTCF acquired its cohesin loop-halting function remains unclear. We performed interspecies domain-swap experiments, replacing the cohesin-interacting N-terminus of mouse CTCF with orthologous sequences from the fruit fly Drosophila (arthropod), Branchiostoma (chordate), and the inshore hagfish (jawless vertebrate). The hagfish N-terminus halted cohesin, whereas the invertebrate CTCF N-termini did not. Consistently, Micro-C maps from hagfish tissues revealed stripes associated with convergently oriented CTCF sites, a characteristic signature of cohesin-loop halting. Notably, cohesin enrichment at promoters and enhancers was more pronounced in hagfish than in jawed vertebrates. Our findings indicate that CTCF-mediated cohesin loop anchoring most likely evolved in the common ancestor of extant vertebrates and was further strengthened in jawed vertebrates.
